previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis was admitted with chest pain and hyperkalemia. Initial evaluation revealed fluid overload and elevated potassium, managed with medical therapy and dialysis. Her left arm arteriovenous fistula, previously complicated by steal syndrome, was evaluated with a fistulogram, which revealed stenosis. During attempted angioplasty, the fistula ruptured, causing a hematoma that required surgical evacuation. The fistula was rendered nonfunctional, and a temporary right subclavian dialysis line was placed, later converted to a tunneled catheter. Her chest pain resolved, potassium normalized, and INR stabilized after warfarin adjustment. She was discharged home with instructions to protect her right arm for future fistula creation, continue medications, monitor weight, and follow up with transplant surgery and nephrology.

previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis was admitted with chest pain and hyperkalemia. Initial evaluation revealed fluid overload and elevated potassium, managed with medical therapy and dialysis. Her left arm arteriovenous fistula, previously complicated by steal syndrome, was evaluated with a fistulogram, which revealed stenosis. During attempted angioplasty, the fistula ruptured, causing a hematoma that required surgical evacuation. The fistula was rendered nonfunctional, and a temporary right subclavian dialysis line was placed, later converted to a tunneled catheter. Her chest pain resolved, potassium normalized, and INR stabilized after warfarin adjustment. She was discharged home with instructions to protect her right arm for future fistula creation, continue medications, monitor weight, and follow up with transplant surgery and nephrology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with right leg pain and ulcers. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started about three weeks ago. My right leg has been really tender, and I noticed an ulcer on the inside. Now there’s another one higher up. My nephrologist told me to come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’re on dialysis, correct? And you’ve been keeping up with your sessions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I haven’t missed any. I’ve also been careful with my diet—no high phosphate foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ve checked your labs, and your potassium is very high—9.9—and your calcium and phosphate are also elevated. This, along with your history, makes us concerned about calciphylaxis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard of that. It’s related to calcium building up in the blood vessels, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And your PTH level is extremely high—1403—so your parathyroid glands are overactive, which is making this worse. We’ll start treatment with dialysis and medications to lower calcium and phosphate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery for the parathyroid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering it. High PTH is fueling the calciphylaxis. Removing the overactive glands may help. We’ll discuss it more after we stabilize you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT angiogram today. It shows severe calcification in your leg arteries, especially on the right. There’s a high-grade blockage in the superficial femoral artery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why my foot is so cold and dusky?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, poor blood flow is contributing. We’re worried about ischemia. We’ll need vascular surgery to open up those arteries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had the parathyroidectomy this morning. All four glands were overactive. Your PTH dropped to 39—that’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but now we have a new concern—your calcium is dropping. Your bones are ‘hungry’ after years of high PTH, so they’re pulling calcium from your blood. We’ll need to monitor and replace it carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need IV calcium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll give IV calcium gluconate and also increase calcium in your dialysis baths. We’ll check your ionized calcium every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ionized calcium is 0.92—quite low. We’re giving 4 grams of IV calcium gluconate now. We’ll keep a close eye on this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if not managed. Low calcium can cause muscle cramps or heart issues. But we’re on top of it. You’re also on calcitriol and calcium pills to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just came back from the procedure. We did an angioplasty and stenting on your right iliac and femoral arteries. We also did an atherectomy to remove plaque.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it help the blood flow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partially. Unfortunately, some plaque broke off and went downstream, blocking smaller vessels in your foot. Your foot is still poorly perfused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the pain might not get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on heparin, Plavix, and aspirin to prevent more clots. But yes, the pain is still significant. We’ll adjust your pain meds and may involve the pain service.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We had to take you back for another procedure. There was a pseudoaneurysm in your left groin and more blockages. We placed three stents and gave tPA to dissolve clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the blood flow better now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We restored some flow, but your foot is still cool and dusky. The vascular team will wait to see how much tissue demarcates before deciding if you need a below-knee amputation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s scary to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But we’re doing everything to save your limb. The good news is your calciphylaxis lesions are responding to intralesional sodium thiosulfate injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The ones they gave me yesterday? They did feel a little better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, dermatology will continue those as outpatient. We stopped IV sodium thiosulfate because it was lowering your calcium too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ionized calcium is now 1.11—much better. We’re reducing the IV calcium but will keep monitoring daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Your foot still needs close monitoring, and we need your INR stable. You’re back on warfarin after surgery—goal is 2.5 to 3.5 because of your mechanical valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember—my valve needs strong anticoagulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your INR was 3.4 this morning—perfect. We’ll keep it there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a skin biopsy. It confirmed calciphylaxis—calcium deposits in small blood vessels, no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s a vascular calcification issue. That’s why we’re focusing on calcium balance and wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your foot isn’t improving much. Vascular surgery still wants to wait and see how much tissue becomes non-viable before deciding on amputation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared of losing my leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But rushing to amputation isn’t always best. We want to preserve as much limb as possible. Your pain is better with the new meds, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the OxyContin and Dilaudid help a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep that regimen. Pain worsening could mean more ischemia, so we’ll watch closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a PICC line today so we can give IV meds safely. We also did another biopsy to confirm the calciphylaxis diagnosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the PICC for the calcium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly, and for antibiotics if needed. Your MRSA screen was negative, so no infection there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Hemoglobin is 8.2—we gave one unit of blood earlier when you were fatigued. You’re on Epogen during dialysis to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel less tired now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Your dialysis is helping clear toxins and balance electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge soon. You’ll go to extended care for wound care and IV calcium support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still need IV calcium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily checks. If ionized calcium drops below 1.1, you’ll get IV calcium. It may take weeks for your bones to stop being ‘hungry.’

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my leg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vascular surgery will see you as outpatient to decide on amputation. Dermatology will continue the sodium thiosulfate injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound care will involve daily Xeroform dressings. Keep the area clean and avoid trauma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay on OxyContin 30mg twice daily, Dilaudid for breakthrough pain, and gabapentin. If pain worsens suddenly, call vascular surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to extended care. Keep monitoring your weight—call if it goes up more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for everything. I’m nervous but ready to move forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot, but you’re on the right path. Follow up with nephrology, vascular, and dermatology. We’ll be checking on you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. You’re strong, and we’re here for you.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis was admitted for worsening right leg pain and ulcers, found to be due to calciphylaxis and severe peripheral arterial disease. She had markedly elevated PTH, leading to a parathyroidectomy, after which she developed hungry bone syndrome with symptomatic hypocalcemia requiring IV calcium replacement and close monitoring. A CT angiogram revealed critical stenosis in the right femoral artery, prompting angioplasty and stenting, complicated by distal embolization and persistent foot ischemia. Despite interventions, her right foot remained cool, dusky, and painful, with vascular surgery deferring amputation pending demarcation. Calciphylaxis lesions were managed with intralesional sodium thiosulfate after IV therapy was halted due to worsening hypocalcemia. Pain was controlled with a multimodal regimen, and anticoagulation was optimized for her mechanical valve. She was discharged to extended care with plans for ongoing wound care, calcium monitoring, and outpatient follow-up with vascular and dermatology teams.
